title: Design Patterns Software Engineering Interview Test

questions.prompt:
A reporting tool must run against either SQL Server or PostgreSQL. The provider is chosen once at startup. For each query the code needs a connection, a command and parameter objects, and these must all come from the **same** provider: a SQL Server command used with a PostgreSQL connection fails at runtime. Today every query method contains its own `if (provider == ...)` branch that creates the three objects.

Which pattern best fits this pressure?
options: Abstract Factory: one factory object per provider creates the connection, command and parameters, so the provider choice is made once
Factory Method: each report class overrides one creation hook, so its subclasses decide which connection class to instantiate
Builder: a fluent builder collects the provider settings step by step and validates the whole combination in a final Build call
Prototype: a configured template connection is cloned for every query, so provider settings are copied instead of rebuilt

rubric.point: Selects Abstract Factory (several related products that must vary together as one family).

questions.model: **Abstract Factory.** Several product types (connection, command, parameter) must vary together and stay compatible. One concrete factory per provider creates the whole family, so the provider decision lives in one place instead of in every query method. Factory Method varies only one product, and Builder and Prototype do not address family compatibility.

options: Memento: snapshot the whole order before each operation, so a caretaker can restore the previous state on undo
Command: represent each operation as an object holding its inputs, so it can be logged, queued, retried and undone
Strategy: put each operation behind a shared interface, so the support tool can swap the algorithm at runtime
Observer: raise an event after each operation, so audit, retry and undo subscribers can react to it independently

rubric.point: Selects Command (the request becomes an object that can be logged, queued, retried and carry undo/compensation logic).

questions.model: **Command.** Turning each operation into an object with its inputs gives it identity, so an invoker can record it in an audit log, put it on a retry queue and keep a history for undo, with each command knowing how to reverse or compensate its effect. A Memento snapshot of the order cannot reverse a refund already sent to an external gateway, and Strategy and Observer do not make the request itself an object.

questions.prompt:
A map renderer draws about 2 million trees. There are only 20 species. Each species has a large mesh and texture that are identical for every tree of that species and never change at runtime. Each tree also has its own position and scale. In the overview zoom level the whole forest is visible at once. A memory profile shows that each tree object holds its own copy of its species' mesh and texture data, and that this duplication dominates memory use.

Which pattern best fits this problem?
options: Object Pool: rent mesh buffers from a pool such as ArrayPool<T> and return them after each tree is drawn
Prototype: build one configured tree per species and deep-clone it, mesh included, for each placement
Flyweight: share one immutable object per species and keep the position and scale on each tree
Virtual Proxy: give each tree a surrogate that loads its mesh and texture only when first rendered

rubric.point: Selects Flyweight (share immutable intrinsic state; keep extrinsic state per use).

questions.model: **Flyweight.** The mesh and texture are intrinsic, immutable state shared by all trees of a species; position and scale are extrinsic. Sharing 20 species objects instead of 2 million copies removes the measured duplication. A pool lends mutable buffers to one borrower at a time, deep-cloning keeps the duplication, and a virtual proxy only defers loading, which does not help when every tree is visible.

questions.prompt:
A `PaymentService` has methods such as `ProcessStripeChargeAsync`, `ProcessStripeRefundAsync`, `ProcessPayPalChargeAsync` and `ProcessPayPalRefundAsync`. The business is adding a new provider (bank transfer) **and** a new kind of payment operation (partial refund), and both lists are expected to keep growing. Every operation makes sense with every provider. Retry and logging code is copied into every method.

In an interview, a candidate is asked which pattern they would use. Name the pattern, explain how it changes the cost of adding a provider and adding an operation, and say why simply injecting one `IPaymentGateway` implementation through DI is not, on its own, the same thing. Also state one limit of the pattern in this design.

rubric.point: Names Bridge.
Identifies two independently varying dimensions (operation type and provider) that currently multiply as providers × operations.
Explains the structure: an operation (abstraction) hierarchy holds a gateway (implementor) interface and delegates to it through composition rather than inheritance.
States a new provider is one new gateway implementation that works with every existing operation.
States a new operation built from existing gateway primitives is one new operation class that works with every provider (shared retry/logging can live in the abstraction).
Explains that injecting one implementation behind one interface varies only one dimension (ordinary polymorphism/Strategy); Bridge needs the second, abstraction-side hierarchy.

Gives a valid limit: a genuinely new primitive changes the gateway interface and every provider; or false independence if some combinations are not supported; or premature when only one dimension varies.

questions.model:
**Bridge.** There are two dimensions, operations and providers, and the current design writes one method per pair, so the count grows as providers × operations and shared retry/logging is duplicated. Bridge splits them: a `PaymentOperation` hierarchy (single charge, subscription, partial refund) holds an `IPaymentGateway` and calls its primitives (authorize, capture, refund). Adding bank transfer is one new gateway class that works with all operations; adding partial refund is one new operation class that works with all providers, and shared retry/logging sits in the operation base.

Injecting one `IPaymentGateway` through DI only varies the provider dimension: that is ordinary polymorphism. It becomes a Bridge because a separate, independently growing operation hierarchy composes with that contract.

**Limit:** Bridge stops the cross-product, not change to the shared contract. An operation needing a new primitive changes `IPaymentGateway` and every provider, and if some combinations are not really supported the design advertises flexibility that does not exist.

questions.prompt:
An e-commerce codebase has two designs whose class diagrams look almost identical: a context object holds a reference to an interface and delegates to it.

- **Design A:** `Order.Ship()`, `Order.Cancel()` and `Order.Pay()` delegate to an `IOrderState`. `PendingState.Ship()` throws because the order is unpaid; `PaidState.Ship()` moves the order to `ShippedState`. Callers never set the status directly.
- **Design B:** `ShippingService.CalculateCost(order)` delegates to an `IShippingCostStrategy` (flat rate, weight-based, zone-based), which is chosen by configuration or a selection policy outside the service.

Name the pattern each design uses and explain what actually distinguishes them, given that the structure is the same.

rubric.point: Design A is the State pattern.
Design B is the Strategy pattern.

State: the delegate represents the object's internal mode and its valid transitions; behavior of the same operation changes as the state changes over the object's lifetime (transitions owned by context or state objects).
Strategy: the delegate is an interchangeable algorithm for one step, supplied/selected from outside as policy; the distinction is intent/reason for change, not the class diagram.

questions.model: Design A is **State**; Design B is **Strategy**. The structure is the same, so intent separates them. In State the delegate *is* the object's current mode: the same `Ship()` call means different things depending on where the order is in its lifecycle, and the states (or the context) drive transitions such as Paid → Shipped. In Strategy the delegate is a replaceable algorithm for one step, picked from outside as a policy; it does not represent a lifecycle and the strategies do not switch each other.

questions.prompt:
Three classes each wrap another object.

A wrapper that implements the interface a client already expects and translates calls to an object with an incompatible interface is a(n) {{translate}}.

A wrapper with the same interface as the wrapped object that adds a responsibility such as logging or metrics, and can be stacked with others in a chosen order, is a(n) {{add}}.

A wrapper with the same interface that decides whether, when or how a call reaches the real object, for example lazy loading, caching or authorization, is a(n) {{control}}.

rubric.point: translate: Adapter
add: Decorator
control: Proxy

source.heading: Choose a Pattern by Intent and Cost

questions.prompt:
A `ReportGenerator` base class runs a fixed sequence: fetch the order, validate it, call an abstract `FormatReportAsync` step, then write an audit record. `PdfReportGenerator` and `CsvReportGenerator` override only the format step.

Two new requirements arrive: the user picks the export format per request, and the same formatting code must be reused inside a different service that already inherits from an unrelated base class.

Should the format variation stay as Template Method or move to Strategy? Justify your choice by contrasting the two.

rubric.point: Chooses Strategy for the format variation.

Justifies: Strategy is a composed object or delegate passed to the context, so it can be selected per request and reused by any class without inheriting from ReportGenerator (does not use the single base-class slot).

Contrasts: Template Method binds the variant to a subclass of the base (choice fixed per object, coupled to hook order/shared state); it fits when the base owns a stable workflow and variants differ in a few hooks.

questions.model: Move the format step to **Strategy**. A formatter is then a separate collaborator (`IReportFormatter` or a delegate) that the generator receives, so it can be chosen per request and reused by the other service without forcing it to inherit from `ReportGenerator`; C# allows only one base class, and that service already uses it. Template Method ties each format to a subclass of the base, fixed when the object is created and dependent on the base's hook order. It is the smaller design only while the base owns the workflow and the variants never need to live outside that hierarchy. The fixed fetch → validate → audit sequence can stay in one class that calls the injected strategy.

questions.prompt:
In a design review for an ASP.NET Core service, a colleague proposes two things:

1. A classical Singleton, `RateLimitConfig.Instance`, with a private constructor, a static field and hand-written double-checked locking. `OrderService` would read `RateLimitConfig.Instance.MaxOrdersPerHour` inside its methods.
2. A `ProductCache` registered with `AddSingleton`. It stores product lookups in a `Dictionary` with no size limit and takes the request-scoped EF Core `DbContext` in its constructor to load missing entries. Many requests run concurrently.

Critique both proposals as you would in an interview: explain what is wrong or risky with each and what you would do instead.

rubric.point: Static access hides the dependency: it is not visible in OrderService's constructor, so it cannot be replaced/mocked in tests and tests share global state.
Recommends a plain class registered with AddSingleton (behind an interface) and injected through the constructor, so the composition root owns lifetime and the container handles creation/disposal.
Notes that if a classical singleton is genuinely needed, Lazy<T> gives thread-safe lazy initialization without hand-written double-checked locking.
Notes that a DI singleton means one instance per root provider/registration, not a global guarantee: a second BuildServiceProvider or direct `new` creates another.
Identifies the captive dependency: the singleton keeps the scoped DbContext alive beyond its scope (scope validation rejects it).
Gives a fix for the captive dependency: create and dispose an explicit scope per load operation (e.g. IServiceScopeFactory), or make the cache scoped / move DB access to a scoped service.
Points out thread safety: one instance serves concurrent requests; the container makes resolution thread-safe but not the Dictionary, so it needs a concurrent/synchronized structure.
Points out unbounded memory: the singleton lives as long as the provider, so the cache needs a size/expiry bound (or a proper memory cache).

questions.model:
**RateLimitConfig.** The static `Instance` hides the dependency: `OrderService`'s constructor does not show it, tests cannot substitute values and they all share global state, and the lifetime is fixed inside the type. I would make it a plain `IRateLimitConfig` class, register it with `AddSingleton`, and inject it into `OrderService` through the constructor. The composition root then owns the lifetime and the container creates and disposes it. The single instance is still only per root provider: calling `BuildServiceProvider` again or using `new` produces another. If a library truly needs a classical singleton, `Lazy<T>` gives thread-safe lazy initialization, so hand-written double-checked locking is unnecessary.

**ProductCache.** Injecting the scoped `DbContext` into a singleton is a **captive dependency**: the first request's context is kept for the life of the app, used after its scope ends and shared across threads. Scope validation rejects this graph. The fix is to create and dispose an explicit scope for each load (via `IServiceScopeFactory`), or to keep DB access in a scoped service. A singleton also serves concurrent requests, and the container does not make its fields thread-safe, so a plain `Dictionary` will race; it needs `ConcurrentDictionary` or locking. Because the singleton lives until shutdown, an unbounded cache keeps growing. It needs a size or expiry limit, for example `IMemoryCache` with a size limit.

questions.prompt:
`OrderService.UpdateStatusAsync` currently calls email, SMS, analytics and warehouse services directly after changing an order's status, and each new channel (push, ERP) means editing it. A colleague proposes the Observer pattern. Two facts are known:

- On the server, all subscribers do asynchronous I/O, and the warehouse notification must complete before the shipping notification starts.
- In the desktop client, each order view subscribes to a `StatusChanged` C# event on a long-lived view model, and memory profiling shows closed views are never garbage collected.

Defend or reject Observer for this design. Explain what it buys, the specific pitfalls in these two situations and how you would handle them, and when Observer would be overkill.

rubric.point: What it buys: the publisher depends only on a notification contract, so subscribers can be added or removed (e.g. via DI-registered observers) without editing OrderService.
Async server subscribers: C# events are synchronous (async void / fire-and-forget is awkward), so use a Task-returning observer interface so completion and failure stay observable.
Failure policy: one throwing handler stops a synchronous event loop; explicit observers must define whether one failure fails the operation, isolating or aggregating failures.
Ordering: Task.WhenAll gives no completion order; the warehouse-before-shipping dependency must be made explicit (sequential awaited loop or explicit workflow), not left to subscription order.
Leak cause: the publisher's delegate list references each subscriber, so a long-lived view model keeps closed views reachable.
Leak fix: the subscribing component unsubscribes with -= (keeping the same delegate instance) when its lifetime ends; weak events only as a fallback when no owner can unsubscribe.
Overkill: with one required dependent (or a fixed, small set that must always run), a direct call is clearer; Observer's indirection makes ordering, lifetime and errors harder to follow.

questions.model:
**Defend, with conditions.** Observer turns `OrderService` into a publisher that depends only on a contract such as `IOrderStatusObserver`, so push or ERP becomes a new registered observer rather than an edit to the service.

**Server.** C# events invoke handlers synchronously, and async handlers end up as `async void` or fire-and-forget, so failures and completion are lost. Use a `Task`-returning observer interface. Define a failure policy: in a synchronous event one throwing handler stops the rest, so observers should either be isolated (catch and log per observer) or have their failures aggregated, with an explicit decision on whether one failure fails the update. `Task.WhenAll` gives no ordering, so warehouse-before-shipping cannot rely on registration order. Await those two in sequence, or move that dependency into an explicit workflow, because it is a business rule and not a notification.

**Client.** Subscribing stores a delegate that references the view in the long-lived view model, so closed views stay reachable and leak. The view that subscribes with `+=` should unsubscribe with `-=` when it closes, keeping the same delegate instance (lambdas must be stored). Weak events are the fallback only when no owner can unsubscribe.

**Overkill** when there is a single required dependent, or a fixed set that must always run in a set order. A direct call is then simpler, and Observer only hides ordering, lifetime and error handling behind indirection.

questions.prompt:
An `Order` aggregate owns its line items. Currently `OrderService.CalculateTotal(order)` sums `order.LineItems` itself. In a refactoring discussion, someone argues: "`Order` has all the data, so by Information Expert, `Order` should also get `SaveToDatabase()` and `SendConfirmationEmail()` methods."

Using GRASP, say where the total calculation, the persistence and the email sending should go, and justify each decision by naming the principles involved.

rubric.point: The total belongs on Order (e.g. Order.Total), by Information Expert: it owns the line items and the invariant.
Explains the coupling benefit: callers no longer reach into Order's internals, and the rule lives in one place instead of being repeated.
Rejects putting persistence/email on Order: it would pull I/O and infrastructure into the domain object, against Low Coupling and High Cohesion.
Puts persistence and email in separate non-domain collaborators (repository, email gateway), justified by Pure Fabrication.
States that Information Expert identifies a strong candidate, not an automatic winner: GRASP principles conflict and the choice depends on which pressure dominates at that boundary.

questions.model:
The **total** moves onto `Order` (`Order.Total`): by **Information Expert**, the object that owns the line items and their invariant computes the result. `OrderService` and other callers then depend only on the total, not on `Order`'s internals, and the rule is no longer repeated.

**Persistence and email** do not belong on `Order`. Putting them there would bring database and email infrastructure into the domain object, violating **Low Coupling**, and mix unrelated reasons to change, violating **High Cohesion**. They go into **Pure Fabrication** classes such as an `IOrderRepository` and an email gateway, coordinated by an application service or controller.

The colleague's mistake is treating Information Expert as absolute. It identifies a strong candidate, but when it conflicts with coupling or cohesion, the pressure at that boundary decides.

Behavioral patterns decide where work belongs and how objects pass control between one another. A sender need not know the receiver, a client need not own every algorithm, and a publisher need not depend on every subscriber. The patterns make those collaborations explicit.

The catalog covers request pipelines, deferred operations, traversal, coordination, snapshots, notifications, state-dependent behavior, interchangeable algorithms, fixed workflows, operations over object structures, and small languages. The names differ, but each pattern answers the same practical question: which object owns the next decision?

```datacorejsx
const { FolderStructureMap } = await dc.require("Assets/components/devbook-folder-map.jsx");
return FolderStructureMap;
```

# Patterns at a Glance

The patterns are grouped by intent, not by quality or complexity. Several often appear in one design because they solve different parts of the same interaction.

| Pattern | Intent | Reach for it when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Chain of Responsibility]] | Pass a request along a chain of handlers, each choosing to handle it or forward it | Several objects might handle a request and the handler isn't known in advance (middleware, escalation) |
| [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Command]] | Encapsulate a request as an object bundling action, parameters, and receiver | Operations need queuing, logging, undo/redo, or replay |
| [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Interpreter]] | Define a grammar and an interpreter that evaluates sentences of a language | A simple, stable language needs evaluation (rules, expressions, DSLs) |
| [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Iterator]] | Provide sequential access to a collection's elements without exposing its structure | Clients must traverse a collection without depending on its internal representation |
| [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Mediator]] | Centralize how a set of components interact, replacing a many-to-many web with one-to-many routing | Objects communicate in complex ways and direct references have become tangled |
| [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Memento]] | Capture and externalize an object's state so it can be restored later, without breaking encapsulation | Snapshots are needed for undo, checkpoints, or rollback |
| [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Observer]] | Define a one-to-many dependency so a subject's change notifies all subscribers | State changes in one object must fan out to many decoupled listeners (events) |
| [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/State]] | Extract state-specific behavior into classes. The context delegates to its current state | Behavior changes with an internal mode and sprawling conditionals obscure the transitions |
| [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Strategy]] | Define a family of interchangeable algorithms behind a common interface | The client must select or swap an algorithm at runtime |
| [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Template Method]] | Define an algorithm's skeleton in a base class, letting subclasses override specific steps | Multiple variants share a fixed overall structure but differ in individual steps |
| [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Visitor]] | Add new operations to an object hierarchy without modifying its classes, via double dispatch | Operations change often while the class hierarchy changes rarely |

# References

- [Behavioral design patterns](https://refactoring.guru/design-patterns/behavioral-patterns)

Creational patterns move object-construction decisions away from the code that uses the result. The pressure is not the `new` keyword itself. It is construction knowledge that is repeated, varies by context, or must preserve an invariant across several objects. Factory Method and Abstract Factory choose implementations, Builder stages complex assembly, Prototype copies an existing configuration, and Singleton constrains lifetime and access.

```datacorejsx
const { FolderStructureMap } = await dc.require("Assets/components/devbook-folder-map.jsx");
return FolderStructureMap;
```

# Patterns at a Glance

The patterns solve different construction problems. The condition in the last column matters more than the pattern name.

| Pattern | Intent | Reach for it when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Factory Method]] | Define an interface for creating an object, but let subclasses decide which concrete class to instantiate. | One product type varies by context, and new variants should arrive as subclasses instead of edits to existing code. |
| [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Abstract Factory]] | Provide an interface for creating **families** of related objects without naming their concrete classes. | Products must stay mutually compatible (a whole Stripe / PayPal provider family swapped together), with new families expected over time. |
| [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Builder]] | Separate construction of a complex object from its representation, assembling it step by step. | Construction needs cross-field validation, computed fields, or a director-driven sequence — beyond what `required` / `init` object initializers cover. |
| [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Prototype]] | Create new objects by copying an existing instance rather than constructing from scratch. | Construction is expensive, or many near-identical variants must be cloned from a template (idiomatically `record with { }`). |
| [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Singleton]] | Ensure a class has only one instance and give it a single global access point. | Exactly one shared instance should serve the whole application — in modern .NET, `AddSingleton<T>()` registration is preferred over the classical static form. |

# Questions

<!-- qard-id: 2c7c6f9d-8162-43be-a7f0-4150803dcf65 -->
> [!qard]- How do Factory Method and Abstract Factory differ?
> Both hide which concrete class is created, but they vary different things. Factory Method lets a subclass decide one product by overriding a creation hook, which inherited creator code such as a shared workflow often calls. Abstract Factory is a separate object, given to its client, that creates a whole family of related products that must work together.
>
> | Aspect | Factory Method | Abstract Factory |
> |---|---|---|
> | What varies | One product returned by an overridable creation hook, often used inside a shared workflow, such as the sender a notification workflow uses. | A family of compatible products, such as a whole Stripe or PayPal provider family that is swapped together. |
> | Mechanism | Inheritance: the creator declares an overridable creation hook such as `CreateSender()`, and concrete creators override it to choose the product. This hook is what defines the pattern. | Composition: the client holds a factory object with one creation method per product and calls it without knowing which family it is. |
> | Where creation sits | In the creator's overridable hook. The same creator often also runs code that uses the product, but it need not. | In a dedicated factory, separate from the code that uses the products. |
> | Adding a variant | A new creator subclass overrides the hook to return a new product, leaving any creator code that uses it unchanged. Creator and product hierarchies grow in parallel only when each concrete product gets its own creator subclass. | A new factory implementation supplies a whole new family. Adding a new kind of product to the family changes the factory interface and every family implementation. |
> | What it protects | Creator code that uses the product, when it exists, stays unchanged while one creation decision varies. | Products obtained from one factory belong to the same family, as long as each factory creates only matching products. |
>
> When neither a subclass-overridable creation hook nor a product family is needed, a standalone factory function is usually smaller than both.
>
> [GoF: Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software](https://cs.gonzaga.edu/faculty/crandall/misc/GoF.pdf) · [GoF: Abstract Factory (InformIT excerpt)](https://www.informit.com/articles/article.aspx?p=1398599) · [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Factory Method#Solution|Factory Method solution]] · [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Abstract Factory#Solution|Abstract Factory solution]] · [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Creational#Patterns at a Glance|Creational patterns at a glance]]

# References

- [Creational design patterns](https://refactoring.guru/design-patterns/creational-patterns)

The Gang of Four catalog names 23 recurring object-oriented design problems and the collaborations that address them. A pattern communicates intent and consequences. It is not a ready-made class diagram. Strategy says that an algorithm varies behind a stable contract, while Observer says that an unknown set of dependents receives notifications. The name is useful only when that pressure exists in the code.

The catalog groups patterns by what varies. Creational patterns move construction decisions, structural patterns compose objects and interfaces, and behavioral patterns assign work or communication. The categories help with recall, but intent decides the pattern.

```datacorejsx
const { FolderStructureMap } = await dc.require("Assets/components/devbook-folder-map.jsx");
return FolderStructureMap;
```

# Choose a Pattern by Intent and Cost

Pattern selection starts from the pressure in the code. The smallest pattern that makes a real variation or responsibility boundary explicit is the candidate, and the condition that would justify deleting it is kept with that decision.

| Pressure | Candidate | What it buys | What it costs | Reject it when |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Construction selects among related product families | [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Abstract Factory]] | Keeps compatible products and construction policy together | Each new family adds a concrete factory; each new product kind adds a product interface and an abstract-factory operation that every concrete factory must implement | There is one concrete family |
| Construction has many ordered or optional inputs | [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Builder]] | Names construction steps and protects invariants | Extra builder type and duplicated API surface | A constructor or options record stays readable |
| Existing interface does not match a consumer | [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Adapter]] | Localizes translation at one boundary | Another abstraction to test and maintain | Both sides are controlled and their contracts can be aligned directly |
| Add behavior around one object without subclass combinations | [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Decorator]] | Composes responsibilities at runtime | Nested wrappers obscure execution order | One direct implementation has no meaningful variants |
| Choose one interchangeable algorithm | [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Strategy]] | Makes policy selection explicit and testable | More types or delegates | A small conditional is stable and clearer |
| Notify unknown dependents about state changes | [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Observer]] | Decouples publisher from subscriber set | Ordering, lifetime, and error handling become indirect | There is one required caller that should invoke directly |
| Encapsulate a request for queuing, undo, or dispatch | [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Behavioral/Command]] | Turns an operation into data with explicit execution | Boilerplate around simple method calls | No delayed, logged, retried, or reversible execution exists |

Similar structure does not imply the same pattern. Proxy and Decorator both wrap an interface, but Proxy controls access while Decorator adds responsibility. State and Strategy both delegate behavior. They differ by intent rather than by who selects the delegate: State transitions may be defined by the context or by the concrete states, while a client usually supplies a Strategy as policy. When the variation disappears, the abstraction no longer earns its cost and can be collapsed.

# Questions

> [!qard]- What is a design pattern?
> A design pattern is a named, reusable solution to a recurring design problem. It describes the problem, how a set of objects collaborates to address it, and the consequences of using it. It is not ready-made code or a fixed class diagram.
>
> - **Name:** a shared word for the design. Saying Strategy communicates that an algorithm varies behind a stable contract.
> - **Problem:** the pressure the pattern responds to, such as an unknown set of dependents that must be notified of state changes (Observer).
> - **Solution:** the roles and their collaboration, adapted to each codebase rather than copied literally.
> - **Consequences:** what the pattern buys, such as replaceable behavior, and what it costs, such as extra types and indirection.
>
> The best-known catalog is the Gang of Four book, which describes 23 object-oriented patterns grouped as creational, structural and behavioral. A pattern is justified only when its problem actually exists in the code; otherwise its indirection is pure cost.
>

<!-- qard-id: 8c5c7210-03f3-4e93-a3d4-c5db11cfc871 -->
> [!qard]- How do the GoF categories (creational, structural, behavioral) relate to choosing a design pattern?
> The three categories group the GoF patterns by the kind of problem they address. They narrow where to look, but the concrete design pressure and each pattern's intent decide which pattern fits.
>
> | Category | Problem it addresses | Examples |
> |---|---|---|
> | Creational | Where construction decisions live: which concrete class is created, how a complex object is assembled, or how instances are copied or limited. | Factory Method, Abstract Factory, Builder, Prototype, Singleton |
> | Structural | How objects and types are composed into larger structures, and how interfaces are adapted or wrapped. | Adapter, Composite, Decorator, Facade, Proxy |
> | Behavioral | How responsibilities and communication are distributed among objects. | Strategy, Observer, Command, State, Template Method |
>
> A category alone cannot decide, because patterns with a similar structure serve different intents. State and Strategy both delegate behavior to another object, but they differ by intent rather than by who selects the delegate: State lets behavior follow the context's current state, with transitions defined by the context or by the state objects, while Strategy makes an interchangeable algorithm a policy that a client usually supplies. The useful starting point is the pressure in the code, such as an algorithm that must vary or an interface that does not match. The pattern whose intent addresses that pressure is the candidate.
>
> [GoF: Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software](https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/design-patterns-elements/0201633612/) · [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Creational/Creational#Patterns at a Glance|Creational patterns at a glance]] · [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Design Patterns#Choose a Pattern by Intent and Cost|Choose a pattern by intent and cost]]

<!-- qard-id: 374c4c3e-1864-4454-84c3-32aa6dac7319 -->
> [!qard]- When does using a design pattern become an anti-pattern?
> A pattern becomes an anti-pattern when the indirection it adds costs more than the variation or responsibility boundary it protects. The pattern name alone never pays for the extra complexity.
>
> Every pattern adds cost:
>
> - more types or delegates to read and maintain
> - an extra hop between a caller and the behavior
> - execution order, lifetime or error handling that becomes harder to follow
>
> Typical signs that the cost is not repaid:
>
> - **No real variation:** an Abstract Factory with only one product family, or a Strategy replacing a small conditional that is stable and clearer.
> - **Trivial construction:** a Builder around values that a readable constructor or options record already handles.
> - **No boundary to protect:** an Adapter between two contracts that the same team controls and could simply align.
> - **Flexibility nobody uses:** a Command wrapper where nothing is delayed, logged, retried or undone, or an Observer with one required dependent that could be called directly.
>
> When the variation that justified a pattern disappears, collapsing the abstraction back into direct code removes its cost.
>
> [GoF: Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software](https://cs.gonzaga.edu/faculty/crandall/misc/GoF.pdf) · [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Design Patterns#Choose a Pattern by Intent and Cost|Choose a pattern by intent and cost]]

<!-- qard-id: f29d53c2-0b44-4cdf-9181-ab4e4a3c89f1 -->
> [!qard]- How do Adapter, Decorator, and Proxy differ despite their similar wrapper shape?
> An object Adapter, a Decorator and a Proxy all wrap another object, but for different reasons. An Adapter translates an incompatible contract into the one a client expects. A Decorator keeps the same interface and adds behavior. A Proxy keeps the same interface and controls access to the real object. A class Adapter adapts through inheritance instead of wrapping an object, so the wrapper comparison describes the object form.
>
> | Aspect | Object Adapter | Decorator | Proxy |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | Interface toward the client | A different interface from the wrapped object's: the one the client expects. | The same interface as the wrapped object. | The same interface as the real object. |
> | Responsibility | Translating calls and data between two incompatible contracts at one boundary. | Adding a responsibility around the call. Several decorators can be stacked at runtime, and their order affects behavior. | Deciding whether, when or how a call reaches the real object. |
> | Effect on a call | It is converted into the wrapped object's operations, and results are converted back. | It normally reaches the wrapped object, with extra behavior before or after. | It may be forwarded, deferred or refused according to the access rule. |
>
> Because their class shapes look alike, the wrapper's responsibility, not its structure, identifies the pattern.
>

GRASP (General Responsibility Assignment Software Patterns) is a set of nine responsibility-assignment principles described by Craig Larman. They answer a concrete design question: which object should know, create, coordinate, or vary this behavior?

The principles are heuristics, so they can point in different directions. Information Expert may place behavior beside the data it needs, while Low Coupling may argue against importing a dependency into that object. The design work is choosing which pressure matters at that boundary.

GRASP applies [[Home/Software Design/Paradigms/OOP]] encapsulation and polymorphism to responsibility assignment rather than prescribing a fixed class structure.

# The Nine Principles

**Information Expert** assigns a responsibility to the object that already has the information required to perform it. An `Order` that owns line items can calculate its total without exposing its internals to an `OrderCalculator`.

**Creator** places construction with an object that contains, records, closely uses, or has the initialization data for the new object. `Order` is a natural creator of the line items it owns.

**Controller** receives a system operation at the boundary and coordinates the use case. It represents the system, a subsystem, or a use-case session rather than performing all domain work itself. An MVC controller can play this role, but the UI pattern and the GRASP principle are not identical.

**Low Coupling** favors assignments that limit how many elements depend on each other and how much they know. Adding an interface helps only when it creates a stable boundary. An interface with no real variation merely moves the dependency.

**High Cohesion** keeps an object's responsibilities strongly related. A controller that validates input, calculates prices, writes SQL, and sends email has absorbed several reasons to change.

**Polymorphism** assigns type-dependent behavior to the types that vary. It replaces a conditional owned by an outsider when new variants are expected to keep arriving.

**Pure Fabrication** introduces a non-domain object when no domain concept is a good home for a responsibility. A persistence mapper or email gateway can improve cohesion without pretending to be part of the business model.

**Indirection** inserts an intermediate object so two elements do not depend on each other directly. The extra hop earns its place only when it absorbs a real variation or communication rule.

**Protected Variations** puts a stable boundary around an identified point of change. A payment-provider contract protects domain code when providers genuinely vary. It is speculative overhead when there is one fixed integration with no separate policy.

# Example: Applying Information Expert

```csharp
// BAD: OrderService calculates total by reaching into Order's data
public class OrderService
{
    public decimal CalculateTotal(Order order) =>
        order.LineItems.Sum(li => li.Price * li.Quantity);
}

// GOOD: Order calculates its own total (Information Expert)
public sealed class Order
{
    private readonly List<LineItem> _lineItems = new();

    public decimal Total => _lineItems.Sum(li => li.Price * li.Quantity);
}
```

`Order` owns both the data and the invariant, so the calculation can remain inside its boundary. A separate service becomes justified when the result depends on information or policy outside that boundary.

# Pitfalls

## Treating Information Expert as an Absolute

Putting every calculation on the object that holds the data can produce a domain object that also performs I/O, coordinates other aggregates, or imports infrastructure concerns. Information Expert identifies a strong candidate, not an automatic winner. Behavior that depends on `Order` state stays on `Order`. Cross-aggregate policy or external communication belongs behind a separate collaborator.

# Tradeoffs

| Decision | Option A | Option B | When A | When B |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Information Expert vs Pure Fabrication** | Put behavior on the class that has the data | Create a service class for the behavior | The rule depends on state and invariants already owned by the object | The work coordinates aggregates or external I/O that does not belong in the domain object |
| **Low Coupling vs Information Expert** | Minimize dependencies via indirection | Assign to the class with the data even if it adds a dependency | When the dependency would cross module or layer boundaries | When the dependency is within the same aggregate and adding indirection adds complexity without benefit |
| **GRASP vs GoF Patterns** | GRASP heuristics for who should own this | GoF patterns for how the collaboration works | Assigning responsibility | Naming a recurring construction, composition, or communication structure |

The better assignment keeps the change-prone rule close to the information it needs without pulling unstable dependencies across a boundary. No single GRASP principle settles every case.

# Example: Polymorphism Replacing Conditionals

```csharp
// BAD: type-switch violates Polymorphism principle
public string GenerateReport(string type, ReportData data) => type switch
{
    "pdf" => GeneratePdf(data),
    "csv" => GenerateCsv(data),
    _ => throw new ArgumentException($"Unknown type: {type}")
};

// GOOD: Polymorphism — each type owns its generation logic
public interface IReportGenerator
{
    string Generate(ReportData data);
}

public sealed class PdfReportGenerator : IReportGenerator
{
    public string Generate(ReportData data) => /* PDF logic */ string.Empty;
}

public sealed class CsvReportGenerator : IReportGenerator
{
    public string Generate(ReportData data) => /* CSV logic */ string.Empty;
}

// Adding a new format = new class, no changes to existing code (Open/Closed)
```

> [!qard]- How does Information Expert reduce coupling?
> Information Expert assigns a responsibility to the object that already holds the information needed to perform it. This reduces coupling because callers no longer reach into that object's data to apply its rule themselves. They depend only on the result, and the rule lives in one place instead of being duplicated by each caller.
>
> **Example:** `Order` owns its line items, so `Order.Total` calculates the total. An `OrderService` that summed `order.LineItems` itself would depend on the internal structure of `Order`, and other callers could repeat the same calculation.
>
> [Craig Larman: Applying UML and Patterns, Information Expert (sample chapter)](https://www.informit.com/content/images/0130925691/samplechapter/0130925691.pdf) · [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/GRASP#The Nine Principles|GRASP principles]] · [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/GRASP#Treating Information Expert as an Absolute|Information Expert limits]] · [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/GRASP#Tradeoffs|GRASP tradeoffs]]

> [!qard]- When should another responsibility-assignment principle override Information Expert?
> Holding the required data makes an object a strong candidate, not an automatic winner. Another principle should prevail when keeping the behavior on the data holder would:
>
> - **Pull infrastructure into a domain object:** behavior that needs I/O, such as persistence or sending email, belongs in a separate collaborator. Pure Fabrication justifies such a non-domain object, for example a mapper or a gateway.
> - **Coordinate several aggregates:** a policy that needs information beyond one object's boundary fits a separate collaborator that coordinates them.
> - **Add a dependency across a module or layer boundary:** Low Coupling favors keeping that dependency out of the object, even though the object has the data.
> - **Give the object unrelated responsibilities:** High Cohesion favors keeping its responsibilities closely related.
>
> Behavior that depends only on the object's own state and invariants stays with that object.
>
> [Craig Larman: Applying UML and Patterns, Information Expert (sample chapter)](https://www.informit.com/content/images/0130925691/samplechapter/0130925691.pdf) · [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/GRASP#The Nine Principles|GRASP principles]] · [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/GRASP#Treating Information Expert as an Absolute|Information Expert limits]] · [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/GRASP#Tradeoffs|GRASP tradeoffs]]

<!-- qard-id: 0743ad5d-e901-45e4-8fc2-a194248e031c -->
> [!qard]- How does GRASP differ from SOLID?
> GRASP and SOLID start from different questions. GRASP, described by Craig Larman, asks which object should own a responsibility: knowing, creating, coordinating or varying a behavior. SOLID asks whether classes, interfaces and their dependencies are shaped so that change stays contained.
>
> | Aspect | GRASP | SOLID |
> |---|---|---|
> | Starting question | Which object should be responsible for this behavior? | Are this class's responsibilities, interfaces, inheritance and dependency direction designed so that change stays contained? |
> | Focus | Assigning responsibilities among collaborating objects while designing how they work together. | Properties of individual classes and interfaces and the direction of dependencies between them. |
> | Content | Nine heuristics: Information Expert, Creator, Controller, Low Coupling, High Cohesion, Polymorphism, Pure Fabrication, Indirection, Protected Variations. | Five principles: Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, Dependency Inversion. |
> | Typical decision | `Order` creates its line items and calculates its own total, because it holds that data. | A class that changes for several unrelated reasons is split, or high-level code depends on an abstraction rather than a concrete detail. |
>
> The two overlap in their goals: low coupling, high cohesion and protection from expected variation. For example, Polymorphism and Protected Variations in GRASP pursue the same goal as Open/Closed in SOLID. They complement each other: GRASP helps decide where behavior goes, and SOLID helps check the shape of the resulting classes and dependencies.
>

Structural patterns organize relationships between objects. They solve different boundary problems: incompatible interfaces, recursive part-whole trees, independently changing dimensions, layered behavior, simplified subsystem access, shared intrinsic state, and controlled access. The right pattern follows from the relationship that must remain stable.

```datacorejsx

return FolderStructureMap;
```

# Patterns at a Glance

These patterns can share nearly identical class diagrams while serving different intents. Decorator and Proxy both wrap an interface. Adapter and Facade both sit at a boundary. Selection depends on whether the design needs translation, simplification, behavior, access control, hierarchy, independent variation, or memory sharing. Several may coexist in one system.

| Pattern | Intent | Reach for it when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Adapter]] | Translate an existing interface into the contract a client expects. | A legacy or third-party API cannot be changed, but the client requires another shape. |
| [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Bridge]] | Separate an abstraction from its implementation so both dimensions can vary. | Two independent dimensions would otherwise produce an N×M set of classes. |
| [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Composite]] | Represent part-whole trees through one component interface. | Clients should apply the same operation to a leaf or a group. |
| [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Decorator]] | Add behavior through same-interface wrappers. | Optional behaviors need explicit composition without subclassing. |
| [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Facade]] | Present a high-level entry point over a complex subsystem. | Several clients repeat the same subsystem workflow. |
| [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Flyweight]] | Share immutable intrinsic state across many fine-grained objects. | Retained duplicate state is a measured memory cost. |
| [[Home/Software Architecture/Patterns/Design Patterns/Structural/Proxy]] | Control access through a same-interface surrogate. | Access must be deferred, cached, authorized, or made remote without changing clients. |
